plain_text:
Being on WBAU with Hank Shocklee and Flava
Flav played a pivotal role in your early career.
Can you say more about those early days?

plain_text:
All those hours Hank and Flav and I spent in
the WBAU studio were just a part of Public
Enemy's origin. It was also the wherewithal
of Bill Stephney that made it all work, along
with what we were doing with Spectrum
City and, later, Andre Brown (aka Doctor
Dre, who went on to host “Yo! MTV Raps”). It
was like the meeting of the hip-hop minds,
laying a foundation that will never leave us.

plain_text:
You’ve said you originally put together
1984’s “Public Enemy #1” on two tape
decks and a Roland 8000 drum machine.
How has hip-hop or your approach to
it changed as technology changed?

plain_text:
Right now, AI is mind-blowing. Hip-hop has
always made music out of technology, out
of recordings and turntables manipulated
to make new sounds no one ever
heard before. So, AI puts us right back
at square zero, where we're creating
through technology again. It's something
I believe we have to learn to dance with
instead of trying to negate or eliminate.

plain_text:
“Fear of a Black Planet” was the second
hip-hop record added to the National
Recording Registry. What did that
mean for you and Public Enemy?

of a Black Planet” was our statement
about the hip-hop we saw and heard
around the world when we toured. It’s our
dissertation of rap words and beats.

plain_text:
You recently became a member of the
National Recording Preservation Board. Why
is the board's work important to you?

It's important for people who love the music
and the art to be a part of recognizing the
work of artists who may not be known
to someone outside of that industry
or genre. As part of an art form that is
historically misunderstood, I'm honored to
be able to be a voice for it on the board.

plain_text:
You're an author, film producer, radio
host, recording artist, visual artist
and activist. You've been called
an icon and a revolutionary. What
would you like your legacy to be?
